idea: Harrison's longitude problem as a plot: Natural Earth meridians as thin lines, with the 1714 Longitude Act's 'Within half a degree' as the only caption. The shirt for people who know that a minute of timekeeping error was 18 nautical miles of shipwreck.

Every coastline is longer when you measure it with a shorter ruler: Natural Earth's Britain drawn five times at 200, 100, 50, 25 and 12 km divider steps, each wigglier and bigger, captioned 'How long is the coast? Depends who's asking.' Mandelbrot's coastline paradox, visible at a glance.

A great-circle plot of a Mercator-distorted world: Natural Earth countries drawn as true-size circles (Tissot indicatrices) across a Mercator grid, swelling toward the poles. Caption: 'Every circle is the same size.' A quiet argument about who gets to be big on the map.

The true size of Africa: Natural Earth outlines of the US, China, India, Europe and Japan packed inside Africa's outline like a jigsaw, in one ink, captioned 'Fits.' Short, a bit smug, and corrects a map error everyone half-remembers.

A terrain-line 'Joy Division' ridge plot of public-domain SRTM elevation data for the Himalaya, 80 stacked profile lines hiding each other, with a single small caption 'Everest, 8,849 m. Still being measured.' Looks like a record sleeve, reads as a mountain.

Voronoi map of the world's capitals from Natural Earth: every point on land coloured by its nearest capital as outlined cells, captioned 'Nearest capital.' Shows that borders are an argument and distance is a fact; a map you can find your own cell on.

Rhumb line versus great circle: the flight from Lisbon to New York drawn both ways on a Mercator grid, the curved shortest path and the straight constant-bearing path, captioned 'Straight is not shortest.' For anyone who has ever been told the obvious route.

A compass rose generated from the 32 points of the wind, each point labelled in the old sailor's names (north, north by east, north-north-east...) in small type, with 'Which way?' at the centre. Pure type and geometry, a classic of wayfinding made precise.

The graticule of places named 'Springfield': a Natural Earth US outline with dots for every Springfield, Franklin, Washington and Georgetown, from open GeoNames data, captioned 'Unoriginal, everywhere.' A funny and true portrait of how settlers named things.

Dymaxion-style unfolding: Natural Earth continents projected onto an icosahedron net and cut flat, captioned 'There is no flat Earth. There are only choices.' For people who like their maps with an admitted compromise.

Dead reckoning simulation: 200 ships start from the same harbour with a tiny random compass error and speed error, their tracks fanning out across the ocean over thirty days, captioned 'Same heading. Different oceans.' A chart of how small mistakes become continents.

Night-sky wayfinding: Hipparcos public-domain star positions plotted as the polar sky with Polaris at centre, 24 hours of star trails as concentric arcs, captioned 'The one fixed point.' A navigator's shirt that is also a beautiful long exposure.

Tide-chart of the Bay of Fundy: a sine-sum plot of the 16 m tidal range drawn as water level over a month using the published harmonic constituents, captioned 'Twice a day the bay breathes out.' Data-built, calm, and strangely moving.

Polynesian wayfinding swell map: wave-interference lines radiating from a handful of Pacific islands from Natural Earth, crossing in moire patterns, captioned 'They read the water.' Honours a navigation method that needed no instrument, and the pattern is gorgeous.

All the rivers of the world as a tree: Natural Earth river lines stripped of land, coastlines removed, in line weight by Strahler order, captioned 'Water finds the way.' The continents emerge only as drainage, like a vein map of the planet.

Dutch polders and the Zuiderzee: a code-drawn contour of the Netherlands elevation below sea level, with the land below zero hatched, captioned 'Below the line.' For people who like a map that shows what shouldn't be there.

Time zones as they are, not as they should be: Natural Earth time zone polygons as slashed offsets from perfect 15-degree strips, with the ragged political borders overlaid, captioned 'Noon is negotiable.' A map joke with a data spine.

Magellan's circumnavigation as a calculated line: the 1519 to 1522 route drawn on a Natural Earth globe viewed from the south pole, with 'Left with 270. Returned with 18.' in small type. A voyage, a fact and a point of view in one image.

A cartogram of the globe resized by the number of undersea cables landing in each country, from open submarine cable data: tiny map, glowing coast. Caption: 'The internet is mostly under water.' Contemporary exploration and geography combined.

Contour lines of Mount Fuji from public elevation data, drawn at 100 m intervals in a ring pattern that doubles as a fingerprint, captioned 'Know where you stand.' Surveying as portraiture; one ink works perfectly for contours.
